source.title: Scaling laws for amplitude surrogates
source.authors: H. Bahl; Victor Bres'o-Pla; A. Butter; J. Ramirez

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study tests scaling laws in amplitude-surrogate regression, a different task and training setting from language-model pretraining.
record.gate_note: This study does not test language-model cross-entropy, language-model extrapolation, compute-optimal language-model allocation, or downstream language-model performance. It directly measures test-loss scaling for amplitude surrogates, which bears on V5, and examines how fitted scaling behavior varies with process and architecture, which bears on part of V7. It also reports learned uncertainty distributions and intrinsic-dimension estimates; those are not rows for the listed versions.
record.test_reason: The study fits power laws to test MSE of amplitude-surrogate regressors as data, parameters and compute vary, across 11 particle processes and two architectures. This is a non-text setting, so it bears on V5. It also shows exponents shifting with process, architecture and training choices, which bears on V7. It does not touch language-model loss (V1), extrapolation to much larger language-model runs (V2), compute-optimal allocation (V3), shape at fixed parameter count (V4) or downstream tasks (V6).
record.authors_conclusion: The record is mostly right. In addition, the authors find dataset size the dominant factor, then compute, with network size minor (no gain past about 1e4 parameters). They say the exponents are not peculiar to one architecture: LLoCa boosts performance on permutation-symmetric processes without much change in coefficients, though they call their architecture analysis limited. They propose using a low-cost run plus the 4/d bound to get an upper bound on the resources needed.
record.recipe_differences: This is a study of physical-amplitude regression using MLP-I and LLoCa-Transformer models, primarily with MSE or heteroscedastic loss. It does not use language-model pretraining or held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary with process complexity and particle multiplicity, architecture, dataset size, and optimization choices. The authors report hyperparameter sensitivity for LLoCa-Transformer, a coarse learning-rate scan causing a final-point loss increase in one curve, and effects of the learning-rate scheduler and weight regularization.

fits_no_version.finding: Fitted αD and αC exceed or match a lower bound of 4/d, where the intrinsic dimension is d=3n_f−4. Learned last-layer representations recover d.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Scaling exponents are bounded by the intrinsic dimension of the data manifold (Sharma & Kaplan), and here that dimension is fixed by the number of external particles.

record.problems: The authors limit their conclusions to the studied training ranges and partonic leading-order processes. They note that the LLoCa-Transformer optimization was difficult, hyperparameter scans may have been too coarse, and some final-point curve behavior resulted from learning-rate selection. Fit uncertainties are based on an assumed 10% relative uncertainty on test losses and do not include possible gains from further hyperparameter optimization.
record.rows_left_out: The paper reports additional separate plotted curves for fixed network sizes, dataset sizes, and compute budgets in Figures 1–4 and 8, and Appendices A.2–A.4. These are not individually transcribed here; the retained rows capture the text-described trends and the reported exceptions. The remaining intrinsic-dimension estimates and learned-uncertainty distribution results are not outcomes for the listed claim versions.

untested.parts: All of it: language-model pretraining loss.
All of it: extrapolation across orders of magnitude for language models.
All of it. N and D are hand-picked per compute budget; no compute-optimal allocation is fitted.
All of it. Shape is not varied at fixed N, since the width-to-length ratio is kept constant.
Image and video models, repeated data, fine-tuning and transfer.
Parameter-counting conventions, alternative fitting methods, and disagreements between published language-model laws.

missing.what: A constant learning rate gives significantly worse scaling than cosine annealing, which the authors say contrasts with language-model findings. This is a training-schedule dependence relevant to V7.
Numeric fitted exponents for qq̄→tt̄H (αC about 2–3.7, αD about 1.7–1.9, αN about 0.6–1.85) and for other processes. The rows say 'figure only' although Tables 2–15 give values.
Under the L1 metric, slopes are roughly halved compared with MSE. The exponent depends on the loss or metric choice.
Scaling is reported as insensitive to batch size from 2^6 to 2^16.

record.verdict_notes: This is a T3 non-language-model setting. Most 'partial' states in the record wrongly treated bottleneck plateaus as failures, although V5 explicitly allows them. R10 is extrapolation, but within regression and modest scale, so it is not linked to V2. The study cites both original sources but is not one of them.

versions.untested_parts: Language-model held-out pretraining cross-entropy scaling in parameters, tokens, or compute.
Extrapolation from small language-model runs to much larger language-model runs.
Compute-optimal parameter and token allocation for language models.
Architecture comparisons at a fixed parameter count; the reported MLP-I and LLoCa-Transformer comparisons do not use the same parameter count.
Image and video models, repeated-data training, fine-tuning, and transfer are not studied; the tested setting is amplitude-surrogate regression.

The study does not test language-model exponent disagreements, compute-optimal allocation, or alternative fitting methods. It does examine scaling variation across amplitude processes, architectures, and some training choices.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.size_stated: 1 million parameters for the compute-scaling study
rows.operation_detail: Varied training FLOPs and measured test MSE for qq̄ → t t̄ H.
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports power-law decrease, plateaus for Dtrain = 102 and 104, and a substantially smaller slope for C ≲ 1011 FLOPs.
rows.note: The text says additional compute benefits the largest dataset only beyond approximately 1014 training FLOPs.
rows.check: State should be observed, not partial. The plateaus at Dtrain=1e2 and 1e4 occur where data is the bottleneck, which V5's framing allows. Fitted αC is 2.1–3.7 (Table 2). For V7, the shallower slope below about 1e11 FLOPs is a bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Varied training dataset size and measured test MSE for qq̄ → t t̄ H.
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports power-law scaling and a visible plateau for NMLP = 102.
rows.note: The study says increasing network size beyond the small-network setting only slightly improves the test loss.
rows.check: State should be observed. The text says the loss follows power-law scaling, with fitted αD of 1.7–1.9 (Table 2). The plateau appears only for the smallest network (NMLP=1e2), where network size is the bottleneck. V7 link dropped: no setup dependence is shown here.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Varied parameter count and measured test MSE for qq̄ → t t̄ H.
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports power-law-like curves and says small datasets force the loss into a saturation regime.
rows.note: The results show dataset size limits the gains from increasing parameter count.
rows.check: State should be observed. Power laws are fitted in N, with αN of 0.6–1.85 (Table 2). The weaker exponent at Dtrain=1e2 (0.601) falls below the 4/d bound, which the authors attribute to data limits. That variation is what links the row to V7.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Measured test error while varying compute and dataset size using a heteroscedastic training loss.
rows.value: Figure only; the text says the scaling behavior looks like the MSE-loss results.
rows.note: The paper describes the heteroscedastic and ordinary MSE scaling behavior as the same.
rows.check: No change. Fitted values are in Table 3, for example αD of 1.75–2.24.

rows.subject: LLoCa-Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared test MSE across training dataset sizes with MLP-I on qq̄ → t t̄ H.
rows.measure: Test MSE as a function of dataset size
rows.value: Figure only; the text says LLoCa-Transformer gave no significant advantage and did not follow a power-law relation as neatly as MLP-I.
rows.note: The authors attribute the less regular scaling to optimization and hyperparameter difficulties; the architectures have different parameter counts.
rows.check: The baseline is another architecture, which is acceptable as a comparator. A fitted αD=1.303±0.015 exists (Table 4) but is not recorded. For V7 the row shows that architecture and hyperparameters affect scaling regularity. For V5 the power law holds less neatly.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Measured test MSE against compute and dataset size for the jet-associated Z processes.
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports power-law scaling, with compute scaling constrained by limited data and slopes decreasing with particle multiplicity.
rows.note: The paper presents separate process curves. The text describes the group-level trend and identifies dataset size as a major performance limit.
rows.check: State should be observed. Power laws are fitted for all four processes (Tables 5–8). For V7, αD falls with multiplicity: about 2.0–2.2 for Zg versus about 0.77–0.79 for Zgggg.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Measured test MSE against compute and dataset size for jet-associated diphoton processes.
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports the same qualitative scaling behavior as for qq̄ → tt̄H, with dataset size a major limitation.
rows.locator: Section 5, Figure 8; Appendix A.3, Figures 14 and 15
rows.note: The study reports separate curves for the two processes.
rows.check: State should be observed. Fitted αD is 1.30–1.46 for γγg and 0.94–0.99 for γγgg (Tables 14–15).

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Measured test MSE against compute and dataset size for electroweak multiboson processes.

conditions.value: qq̄ → WZ, qq̄ → WZg, qq̄ → WWZ, and qq̄ → WZgg

rows.value: Figure only; the text reports power-law scaling and says dataset size is an important limit, while network size has a minor role in the studied range.
rows.locator: Section 5, Figure 8; Appendix A.4, Figures 16 and 17
rows.note: The paper presents separate curves for each process. Some compute-scaling curves have a final-point loss increase attributed to a learning-rate scan that was not fine enough.
rows.check: State should be observed. Power laws are fitted for all four processes (Tables 10–13). The final-point increase is covered separately by R12.

rows.subject: LLoCa-Transformer
rows.operation_detail: Compared dataset-size test-MSE scaling with MLP-I on qq̄ → Zgggg.
rows.measure: Test MSE as a function of dataset size
rows.value: Figure only; the text reports the same αD behavior with particle multiplicity, but a much smaller Ddata,c and flat performance improvement for each Dtrain.
rows.note: The paper says this transformer result contrasts with its qq̄ → tt̄H result and is more stable against hyperparameter changes.
rows.check: State should be observed. LLoCa gives a clean power law with αD=0.911±0.013 (Table 9), versus 0.77–0.79 for MLP-I. Architecture shifts Xc and the exponent, which bears on V7.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Used two small-dataset trainings to predict the dataset size needed to reach a target test loss for gg → γγgg.
rows.measure: Test MSE and predicted dataset requirement
rows.value: Test losses 0.123 and 0.042; two-point αD = 0.94; full-fit αD = 0.939 ± 0.031; XD = 10.7; predicted Dtrain = 1.7 × 104, matching the dataset size where measured loss crosses 10−3. Using αD ≳ 4/d = 0.5 instead predicts 5.6 × 105, overestimating by a factor of 30.
rows.note: The two inexpensive trainings together used less than four minutes of GPU time. The authors condition this procedure on negligible numerical noise.
rows.check: No change. This is a small-run extrapolation within one dataset-size scan, in a non-LM setting. It does not test V2, which concerns language-model runs orders of magnitude larger.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.size_stated: Varied across studies; see Appendix C
rows.operation_detail: Compared fitted dataset and compute scaling exponents across amplitude processes and particle multiplicities.
rows.measure: Fitted power-law exponents αD and αC
rows.value: Figure only; the text says fitted exponents are generally in good agreement with the lower bounds and decrease with external-particle count. The two-particle final-state processes are exceptions with lower coefficients.
rows.note: The authors relate the two-particle exceptions to singularity structure and lower surrogate precision near sharp features.
rows.check: State should be observed. The exponents clearly change with process and particle multiplicity, which is what V7 names.

rows.subject: MLP-I
rows.operation_detail: Examined compute-scaling curves for electroweak multiboson processes.
rows.value: Figure only; the text says the test loss slightly increases at the final compute point, due to a learning-rate scan that was not fine enough.
rows.note: The authors say a finer learning-rate scan would remove this feature.
rows.check: 'Reversed' is misleading. This is a small final-point loss increase that the authors attribute to a coarse learning-rate scan. It shows a curve depending on a training choice, which is V7's point.

relationships.condition: MLP-I amplitude surrogates across 11 partonic processes, with MSE or heteroscedastic loss
relationships.reason: Test MSE follows fitted power laws in compute, data and parameters, plateauing only where another resource is limiting. A two-point fit predicted the data needed for 1e-3 loss (R1–R4, R6–R8, R10).
relationships.display_finding: Test MSE followed compute, data and parameter power laws until another resource constrained progress; a two-point fit predicted the data needed for 10^-3 loss.

relationships.reason: Dataset scaling follows a clean power law with αD=0.911±0.013 (R9).
relationships.display_finding: Dataset scaling followed a power law with αD=0.911±0.013.

relationships.reason: The authors say scaling did not follow a power law as neatly, and they attribute this to hard hyperparameter optimization (R5).
relationships.display_finding: Scaling followed a power law less closely, which the authors attributed to difficult hyperparameter optimization.

relationships.condition: Across processes, architectures and training choices in amplitude regression
relationships.reason: Exponents fall with particle multiplicity and singularity structure. Architecture shifts Xc and regularity, compute curves bend at low FLOPs, and learning-rate choice alters curve endpoints (R1, R3, R5, R6, R9, R11, R12).
relationships.display_finding: Exponents fell with particle multiplicity and singularity structure, architecture changed Xc and regularity, compute curves bent at low FLOPs, and learning-rate choices changed curve endpoints.
